stations.title: Measure blood pressure
stations.sourceRange: Pages 7–17, 20, 25 and 37; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Prepare the subject and cuff correctly
Sequence palpatory and auscultatory measurement
Recognise Korotkoff endpoints and the auscultatory gap
Calculate and report pulse pressure and approximate MAP
Pressure, arterial occlusion and direct versus indirect measurement
Arterial landmarks and alternative cuff sites
Cuff fit, hydrostatic error and comparison between arms
Korotkoff phases and the meaning of silence
Palpatory limits, gaps and endpoint errors
Pulse pressure, MAP weighting and worked comparisons
Read the course BP classification table without diagnosing from one reading
Explain the measurement sequence and instrument function

stations.title: Find and explain heart sounds
stations.sourceRange: Pages 27–33 and assignment p. 37; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Locate the four standard valve auscultation areas
Explain the origin and timing of S1 and S2
Use the stethoscope and describe findings systematically
Distinguish listening areas from anatomical valve positions
S1/S2, systole and isovolumetric phases
S3/S4: filling mechanism and cautious interpretation
Sternal angle and all four valve listening areas
Stethoscope acoustics and troubleshooting
Integrate timing, anatomy and a defensible practical report

stations.title: Record and interpret an ECG
stations.source: ECG Appl Physio Class 7.ppt + ECG Eng Appl Physio Assignment.ppt
stations.sourceRange: Main slides 5–30, 36, 52–61; all four assignment slides; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Position ten electrodes to obtain twelve leads
Read paper speed, gain, waves and intervals
Calculate rate and assess sinus rhythm
Determine frontal axis and recognise standard lead territories
Leads versus electrodes and the three bipolar limb views
Hexaxial directions and frontal versus horizontal views
Electrode landmarks, skin contact and recording quality
Paper speed, gain and millimetre-to-unit conversions
P/QRS/T, PR segment versus interval, QT and ST
Regular and irregular rate calculations with explicit calibration
Apply all five sinus-rhythm criteria, not rate alone
Describe unfamiliar rhythm strips before naming a diagnosis
Axis quadrants, net QRS polarity and lead-II refinement
Equiphasic-axis construction and the local assignment
Lead territories and avoiding overdiagnosis

stations.title: Read a spirometry trace
stations.sourceRange: Slides 6–24; final exercise slide 24; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Explain an acceptable forced-expiration manoeuvre
Identify measurable lung volumes on a calibrated trace
Calculate corrected VC and percentage of predicted
Calculate FEV1/FVC and interpret patterns cautiously
What a spirometer records and why the manoeuvre matters
Tidal and reserve volumes on a tracing
VC, IC, FRC and TLC: definitions and sums
Use the paper's time and volume scale, not screen dimensions
Temperature correction and percentage predicted
FEV1, VC/FVC denominators and ratio arithmetic
Obstruction versus restriction and the incorrect TLC slide
Work the final exercise: order, units and quality checks

stations.title: Count red blood cells
stations.sourceRange: Slides 8–10, 13–15 and 19–23; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Choose RBC-preserving diluent and dilution
Identify the RBC counting area and boundary convention
Derive RBC concentration from counted volume
Recognise loading and sampling errors
Microscope parts, magnification and illumination
Find the chamber grid safely and focus at the right power
Derive the central-grid dimensions rather than memorising a multiplier
RBC pipette identification and dilution logic
RBC concentration calculations and altered dilution
Boundary rules, chamber loading and systematic count errors
Course RBC ranges, units and limits of interpretation

stations.title: Count white blood cells
stations.sourceRange: Slides 10–17; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Explain Türk’s fluid and WBC dilution
Identify WBC counting volume
Calculate and report total WBC concentration
Distinguish total count, differential and preventable errors
WBC pipette, Türk's solution and dilution
Four corner squares, depth and count units
Total-count calculations, averaging and changed dilution
Mixing, loading, border counting and safe technique
What the total count can and cannot tell you

stations.title: Identify the five WBC types
stations.sourceRange: Slides 3–17, especially morphology 5 and 8–16; exercise 17; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Recognise granulocytes by morphology
Distinguish lymphocytes and monocytes
Calculate a differential and an absolute subtype count
Explain systematic smear sampling and source limitations
Recognise cells in additional course micrographs
Granulocytes, agranulocytes and principal functions
Hematopoietic lineages and formed elements
Course percentages and why size alone is insufficient
100/200-cell differentials and absolute counts
Integrate morphology, relative counts and interpretation limits

stations.title: Read hematocrit / PCV
stations.sourceRange: Slides 1–11; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Explain packed-cell volume and specimen choice
Recognise layers and centrifuge safety
Read a hematocrit reader and calculate PCV
Identify causes of biased readings and interpret cautiously
Packed-cell volume, plasma and the buffy coat
Anticoagulation, sealing, balance and centrifuge settings
Reader alignment, numerator and worked PCV ratios
Relative versus absolute changes and causes listed in the slides
Course ranges and specimen validity

stations.title: Distinguish bleeding and clotting time
stations.sourceRange: Slides 12–25; expanded theory sets include additional source pages listed below

objectives.title: Distinguish primary haemostasis from fibrin clot formation
Recognise the bleeding-time endpoint and course convention
Recognise capillary and slide clotting-time endpoints
Handle method dependence and ambiguous instructions safely
Vessel injury, platelet adhesion, activation and aggregation
Primary versus secondary haemostasis and assay limitations
Bleeding-time endpoint, sampling intervals and interpretation
Capillary clotting time: tube, endpoint and conflicting timer instructions
Slide clotting time and the two endpoint descriptions
Platelet number versus function and selective test abnormalities
Timing resolution, specimen validity and practical safety
